claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units modestly as a stopgap.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units.
SDU tenants pay a per-square-foot premium of 15 to 25 percent despite lower median rents.
The SDU market is not functioning like a normal rental market.
SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households, and public housing waiters.
The average public housing wait is about five and a half years.
Demand for SDUs is highly inelastic, giving landlords little competitive pressure.
Rent control caps increases on sitting tenants and gives households predictability.
The poorest households pay the most per unit of space.
A cap on annual increases would narrow the premium without eliminating supply incentives.
Tighter controls risk reducing SDU supply, which is a real risk.
A strict rent freeze should not be supported.
SDU supply responds to housing shortage rather than rent levels alone.
Existing tenants' security matters more than marginal landlords' returns.
Rent control alone cannot solve the housing problem.
The root cause is the long public housing wait.
Rent control should be paired with supply-side measures.
A cap on annual increases is preferable to a rent freeze.
The policy is a stopgap, not a cure, but better than nothing for 110,000 households.

cites.sentence: About 110,000 households live in flats carved into small cubicles with shared kitchens and bathrooms, and while the median SDU rent is roughly 30 percent below mainstream private flats, tenants actually pay a premium of 15 to 25 percent per square foot because space is priced at its most desperate margin [D1p1].
SDU tenants are disproportionately new arrivals, single-parent households and residents waiting for public housing, where the average wait has hovered around five and a half years [D1p2].
For these households the SDU is not a choice but a residual option while the queue moves [D1p2].
Tightening rent control addresses exactly this imbalance by capping how much landlords can raise rents on sitting tenants, giving households predictability while they wait for public housing [D1p2].
The per-square-foot premium of 15 to 25 percent [D1p1]
The goal is not to make SDU landlords rich or poor; it is to stop the premium from growing while the public housing queue remains long [D1p2].
But the risk is overstated in the SDU context because the supply of subdivided units is itself a response to a housing shortage, not to rent levels alone [D1p1].
Moreover, the 110,000 households already living in SDUs [D1p1]
The root cause is the five-and-a-half-year public housing wait [D1p2], and no rent cap will shorten that queue.
A tightened cap buys time and reduces the per-square-foot premium [D1p1]
Without it, tenants absorb the cost of the shortage through the most regressive channel available: paying more per square foot for less space [D1p1].
The evidence shows that SDU tenants pay a per-square-foot premium of 15 to 25 percent [D1p1]
despite being the households least able to afford it, and that they are trapped by a public housing queue averaging five and a half years [D1p2].
The policy is a stopgap, not a cure — but for 110,000 households [D1p1], a stopgap is better than nothing.
